youtube.title: Your JPEG Has 256 Shades. A 14-bit RAW Has 16,384.
youtube.description:
An 8-bit JPEG stores 2^8 = 256 levels per colour channel; a 14-bit RAW stores 2^14 = 16,384 — 64× more per channel (256³ ≈ 16.7 million vs 16,384³ ≈ 4.4 trillion possible RGB values). Many cameras record RAW at 12 or 14 bits (e.g. Nikon lets you pick either). A JPEG also has the camera's white balance and tone curve applied; RAW stores the sensor data and keeps those settings for later.

Why it matters: we simulated (numpy, no compression) a dark sunset sky shot 4 stops under, stored once as 8-bit gamma-encoded JPEG data and once as 14-bit linear RAW data, then pushed both +4 stops. The JPEG sky had 24 green levels vs 190 for the RAW; stretched 16×, the JPEG bands and its histogram turns into a comb (50 of 74 values empty). The RAW stays smooth.

Sources: Wikipedia (Raw image format, JPEG), Cambridge in Colour (bit depth, posterization), Nikon Z 7 manual (12/14-bit NEF).
